sections.h2: Choosing a route for a Stow sale
sections.html:
Match the sale route to what is wrong with the house, if anything. A well-kept Stow home does fine on the open market. A house with a dying roof, a difficult tenant or an estate still in progress may fit a buyer who takes it unrepaired.

  • Agent listing: photos, open houses, a buyer's inspection and the repair requests that come after it.
  • Owner-sold: you set the price and handle the disclosure form and deed paperwork.
  • Direct cash sale: one buyer, one walkthrough, and a quicker trip to the county transfer desk.

Each route ends with a deed filed through the county, so bring in a title company or attorney at the beginning.

Stow sits on the Summit and Portage county line next to Akron, on 17.09 square miles of land. Population was estimated at 33,941 on July 1, 2025, down 1.6 percent from April 2020. Most homes are owner-occupied. The city lies in the secondary Lake Erie snowbelt, so expect an inspector to spend time on the roof, gutters, furnace and basement.

Sometimes, because of unfinished work. A newer deck, furnace, roof or finished basement often prompts a buyer's inspector to ask for the permit. Gather your records before you list and close anything still open.

The Stow Building Department runs permits and construction inspections, and its online portal accepts forms, inspection requests and contractor registrations at any hour. A call in before 9 am gets same-day inspection, and electric and plumbing visits happen on Monday, Wednesday and Thursday mornings. The department's line is 330-689-2729. Engineering covers drawings and work in the public right-of-way, and answers at 330-689-2719.

Sanitary sewer permits are not issued by the building office. Summit County's Department of Sanitary Services, 1180 S Main Street in Akron, handles them, so phone that office with any sewer lateral question before closing.

sections.h2: What happens at the Summit County Fiscal Office
sections.html:
Summit County's Property Transfer Department reviews the legal description and signs off on the conveyance. A DTE 100 statement of value goes with each deed, or a DTE 100 (EX) if an exemption applies. Papers in by 3:30 PM can be approved the same day.

The county's fee page lists three charges to expect at closing:

  • Conveyance Fee: $4.00 per $1000 rounded up to the next $100 of the sale price.
  • Lot Fee: 50 cents per lot contained in the legal description.
  • Basic recording: $34.00 for two pages, $8.00 for each additional page.

Ohio Revised Code 322.02 puts the county transfer tax on the grantor, paid to the auditor when the deed is delivered. Ask your closing agent to compare the settlement statement with these charges.

Houses with up to four units need the state property disclosure form under Ohio Revised Code 5302.30. Give each prospective buyer a signed, dated copy early, since one who receives it late can rescind in writing. Questions cover water, sewer, structure and hazards such as radon and lead paint.

Answer each item honestly. If you truly lack the facts, the statute lets you give a good-faith approximation.

sections.h2: Selling a Stow house with a tenant or from an estate
sections.html:
You can sell a rental with the tenant staying or with a move-out date in the contract. Share the lease and the deposit ledger with the buyer, and keep meeting your landlord duties until title changes hands.

With an inherited house, the first question is who may legally sign. Ask the probate court and the Fiscal Office which affidavit or certificate takes title out of the decedent's name, and consult an Ohio probate attorney about anything left. After that the sale follows the usual steps.

sections.h2: Paperwork to line up before closing
sections.html: A Stow closing runs more smoothly when the following are ready ahead of time. Gather your permit records and ask the Building Department about anything still open. Sign and date the disclosure form for each buyer who asks. If the house has a sewer lateral issue, call Summit County Sanitary Services early. Ask the closing agent to prepare the deed with the DTE 100 so it reaches the Property Transfer Department before 3:30 PM and can be approved that day. Confirm the conveyance fee, lot fee and recording charge against the settlement statement, and ask who pays what before you sign. For a tenant-occupied house, have the lease, deposit ledger and any vacate date ready. For an inherited house, confirm the probate paperwork first.

sections.h2: When a cash offer is worth considering
sections.html:
A direct buyer fits an inherited house with put-off repairs, a tenant-occupied rental, or an owner who has relocated and pays two sets of bills. When a roof or sewer line is nearly done, an as-is purchase removes the repair decision.

Set any offer against a listing's net after commission and repairs. Ask who pays the transfer charge, how long title work takes and what happens if the buyer backs out, and put each answer in the contract.

faqs.q: Who pays the county transfer charge on a Stow sale?
faqs.a: You do, as the seller. The county transfer tax falls on the grantor under Ohio Revised Code 322.02, and the auditor side of the Summit County Fiscal Office collects it when the deed arrives.

faqs.q: What inspections does the City of Stow perform?
faqs.a: Permit inspections on construction work, with same-day service for calls before 9 am. Check with the Building Department at 330-689-2729 about your address, and plan on the buyer ordering a private inspection.

faqs.q: Which office records a Stow deed?
faqs.a: A Stow address falls under Summit County, which means the Fiscal Office records the instrument after the transfer step. Ask for the per-page recording charge when you schedule the closing.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Stow house that has a tenant?
faqs.a: Yes. Give the buyer the lease and the deposit ledger, or put a move-out date in the contract. Your landlord duties last until title changes hands.

faqs.q: What if I inherited a house in Stow?
faqs.a: First find out who may legally sign. The probate court and the Fiscal Office can name the affidavit or certificate that clears the decedent's name, and a probate attorney can handle the rest before you accept an offer.
